text:
Yes — present the monthly version, but not as if you’ve changed your mind about the need. Present it as the fundable first phase of the weekly proposal.

Refusing to present it gets the clients nothing. Pretending monthly is what they need costs you your integrity and teaches the trustees that the problem was smaller than you said. The stronger move is to hold both facts at once: weekly is the actual need; monthly is what can be funded today.

Before Thursday week, tell your manager: “I’ll present the monthly supper as a pilot, but I need to be clear that the underlying need is weekly.” If she wants an easy meeting, that is still easy. It just doesn’t erase the truth.

At the meeting, I’d say something like: “My original proposal was weekly because isolation at this centre is weekly. People are alone between appointments. A monthly supper will not solve that, but it is real support and it can start now. I’m asking you to fund six monthly sessions, with a simple evaluation plan: attendance, feedback, volunteer hours, and whether people return or access other services. I’d also like a review date and a clear condition for expanding to weekly if the evidence supports it.”

Then ask directly: “What would need to be true for weekly to become fundable?” That changes the conversation from “nice extra” to “what evidence, partnership, or budget line gets us there?” It also makes the two trustees own their objection rather than just dismissing you.

Practically, make the monthly session as visible as possible: a sign-in sheet, photos if consented, a one-page summary afterwards, and a short anonymised story. You already know the Eritrean man who sits in the corridor; that kind of detail, respectfully used, is what makes trustees feel the gap.

If your manager insists that you present monthly as if you now think it is the right answer, don’t. Ask her to present the funding compromise and let you speak to the service need. You can still be the person who makes it work.

Take the monthly supper. Keep the weekly proposal alive. Make the trustees approve a path, not just a smaller version.

Put the cut number at the top as the amount trustees are being asked to approve. The agenda line should be the decision that can actually pass, not the figure that makes you feel most honest but gets the item killed. If you put the full number as the ask, you are likely to walk away with nothing, and the people who might have been covered by the third get nothing too.

But do not let the full need disappear. Label the item clearly as a first phase or pilot. For example:

“Approval of monthly fare-support pilot: £[cut amount], covering approximately one-third of current evidenced requests. Full identified need: £[full amount] per month.”

Then include a short paragraph saying this is the urgent minimum because of budget constraints, and that the full list remains documented and will be brought back if funds allow. Attach or append the names, dates, interview letters, and criteria, even if the trustees only approve part of it. That way you are not pretending the need is smaller than it is; you are asking for the largest slice that has a realistic chance of passing.

Also, take the choosing out of your own hands as much as possible. Ask for approval of clear criteria: asylum interviews, legal appointments, medical appointments, households with children, people with no other support, and a monthly cap. If the fund is oversubscribed, the priority should be risk of losing a claim or missing a statutory appointment, not who you happened to speak to first.

Do not tell the clients help is coming until Thursday is over. If the trustees approve the smaller fund, you can say, “A limited fare fund has been approved; we will prioritise by appointment risk.” If they do not, you can say honestly, “It was not approved this time,” rather than having promised something you cannot deliver.

So: print the cut figure as the requested decision, but keep the full figure visible as the true unmet need. That is the most practical way to get something approved without lying to yourself or the people relying on you.

Take the third today. The person you owe the immediate duty to is Mrs Adeyemi, not the abstract principle of overturning the clause. If the realistic outcome of pushing is that she gets nothing for months, while a guaranteed one-third pays for a plumber, flooring and a dry room, the humane and professional decision is to take the money.

Do not make it a secret favour, though. Send your manager a short written note now: “Given Mrs Adeyemi’s age, vulnerability, loss of habitable accommodation and urgent need to mitigate damage, I recommend an immediate goodwill/ex-gratia payment of £X today. I will record it as a vulnerable-customer decision. Please confirm authorisation by [time].” If you can, get it stated as without prejudice and not a waiver of her right to complain. If he will only allow it as full and final, try first to get it framed as an urgent interim payment. If he refuses and the choice really is £X today or probably £0, take £X and record why.

Call her before 5 if possible. Don’t settle entirely over her head. Say: “Your claim was declined, but I can secure an immediate goodwill payment of £X today. It would help pay for urgent repairs. The appeal is uncertain and may take time. Do you want me to accept it?” Record her consent. If she cannot be reached and you have authority to act in a vulnerable customer’s best interests, secure the payment and document the reasoning.

After today, raise the underlying problem properly: a maintenance clause that has never been explained and is being used against elderly renewal customers is a fairness issue. That fight can happen later through compliance, complaints, or the ombudsman. But do not gamble her immediate shelter on it today.

Take the money. It is not perfect justice; it is the option that actually helps her tonight.

Go in calm, brief, and fact-based. Don’t make it about your anxiety or about challenging his authority. Make it about the claim, the deadline, and the risk of getting it wrong.

Bring one page: the key policy/fact points, the appeal deadline, and the amount that should be paid. Knock, sit down, and say something like:

> “I need a few minutes before the appeal deadline. I know you floated a goodwill partial payment this morning, but I don’t think that’s the right call. Based on the file, this claim should be paid in full. The facts/policy support it, and if we only offer a partial payment today, we may create a bigger issue later. I’m raising it now because I don’t want us to miss the deadline or make a decision we can’t defend.”

Then give your strongest two reasons only. Don’t over-explain. End with a clear ask:

> “I’m asking you to approve full payment today, or at least let me preserve the appeal while we resolve it.”

If he says the offer comes off the table, don’t panic and don’t immediately argue. Clarify what he means:

> “Just so I understand: are you saying that because I raised this, the partial goodwill offer is withdrawn? Or that we’re making no offer today?”

If he says the offer is withdrawn, say:

> “I understand that’s your decision. My recommendation is still full payment. Because the deadline is today, I need to know exactly what you want communicated. If we’re denying or not responding, please tell me the wording or approve the response.”

If he refuses to give clear direction, say:

> “Then I need a few minutes to document my concern and confirm next steps before the deadline.”

After the meeting, send a short recap email: “Per our conversation, I raised concern that the goodwill partial payment is insufficient and the claim should be paid in full. You directed X. I will proceed accordingly unless you tell me otherwise.” That creates a record without being aggressive.

If he asks you to do something you believe is unlawful, fraudulent, or contrary to regulation, stop and escalate to compliance/legal/HR before acting.

You’re not crazy. Dana’s face matters. It means the policy has a human cost, and you’re right to feel that a “good” compromise can still leave someone you know behind. But I don’t think you should vote against the capped version.

Vote for the cap, because the alternative is almost certainly the £45 fees staying as they are. If the full motion would lose, voting no doesn’t rescue Dana’s £300. It mostly risks leaving hundreds of tenants exposed to future charges, including tenants who may end up in Dana’s position next month. A symbolic no may make you feel less complicit, but it doesn’t make Dana whole; it just makes the overall harm worse.

The better move is to refuse to let the cap be the end of the story. Support it explicitly as harm reduction, while naming its flaw in the room: “This protects people going forward, but it abandons tenants already punished by these fees, including low-income tenants who aren’t on benefits. I’m voting yes, but I want a separate motion or hardship provision for refunds/waivers for people already in payment plans or financial hardship.” If you can, push for an amendment: retrospective relief for anyone on a payment plan, anyone below an income threshold, or a discretionary hardship fund.

Then talk to Dana honestly. Don’t promise her a refund. Say: “The full refund motion probably won’t pass. The cap probably will. I’m pushing for relief for people in your situation, and I won’t pretend the current version is fair to you.” Ask whether she’d be willing to have her case raised anonymously, or whether she wants to make a statement. If not, still raise the principle.

Your job isn’t to be the one pure person who voted no. It’s to get the best achievable result and keep fighting for the people the compromise misses. Dana deserves more than your symbolic loyalty. She deserves you using whatever leverage you have to try to get her £300 addressed, without letting other tenants pay for that loyalty.

You weren’t wrong to be angry that the cap left Dana still paying off old fees. But you were wrong to make voting against the cap the main way of showing that anger.

The cap does something real now: it stops people on benefits being charged and limits fees for everyone else. Your “no” didn’t get Dana £300 back. It only risked weakening a measure that helps other tenants, while doing nothing practical for her. In a tenant panel, the better move would have been to support the immediate relief and then push an amendment: cancel or credit outstanding pre-cap fees, or at least create a hardship review for people like Dana. If you couldn’t vote yes in conscience, abstain and speak explicitly about the injustice to people still paying old charges.

So reply to Dana. Don’t hide from her. You could say something like:

“I’m sorry I didn’t reply. The cap passed, but it doesn’t cancel or refund old fees, which is really unfair, especially for you. I should have pushed harder for that part. I’m going to ask the panel/landlord to write off or credit the old charges. Can we raise it together?”

If she asks how you voted, be honest, but don’t present your vote as solidarity. Say: “I voted against because it left you out, but I think I should have fought for an amendment instead.”

Then do the practical bit. Ask the panel or landlord directly whether old fees can be waived, credited, or frozen. If they say “it’s not retrospective,” ask for a discretionary hardship process. Find out whether other tenants are in the same position and raise it collectively. If the old fees may have been wrongly charged in the first place, get advice from a tenants’ union or Citizens Advice.

Your guilt isn’t the point. Dana’s £300 is. Turn the awkwardness into action.

You’re not wrong to see the capped version as a compromise that abandons the people the fees hurt most. But I wouldn’t push anyone to vote it down.

Your colleague has the better tactical read. If the capped version fails, the most likely result is not that the owners return with refunds; it’s that nothing passes, the current fee regime continues, and the cleaner you’re thinking of keeps paying. To justify killing the cap, you’d need a credible path from defeat to a better deal: owners who fear reputational damage, panel members willing to keep fighting, a public campaign, or a specific alternative already sketched. You’re not describing that. You’re describing a room that has settled and wants to declare victory.

So use your influence to make the settlement less shameful rather than to sink it. Because you’re the minute-taker, do this privately and before the meeting, not from the chair. Go to one or two members who listen to you and say exactly what you said here, but with a concrete amendment: “Pass the cap, but add retrospective relief. Waive or credit the outstanding admin fees for tenants already in arrears or on benefits, at minimum for hardship cases like the cleaner. Create a small refund/credit pool from recent fee income, or set a review in six months to clear legacy charges.”

If you can, give them numbers: how many tenants are still carrying old fees, roughly how much is involved, and how many are on benefits or in hardship. That turns “this is unfair” into “this is a finite, solvable problem.” The cleaner doesn’t need a symbolic defeat of the panel; she needs her balance wiped or reduced. A targeted legacy waiver may be sellable to owners because it is limited, means-tested, and framed as closing off old debts, not reopening the full refund fight.

If they refuse even that, I’d still advise letting the cap pass, because it at least stops new fees hitting the most vulnerable. Then record your concern clearly, keep the evidence, and make next year’s proposal explicitly about legacy refunds. Half a loaf can become a foothold; voting it down is more likely to become no loaf.

Yes — probably out of line, but not because your opinion was wrong.

The problem is your role. If you’re the minutes-taker, you’re seen as part of the panel’s machinery, even if you don’t vote. That gives your words extra weight. When you say “this is a sell-out and you should vote against it,” it can sound less like a personal view and more like an official or insider judgment. That’s likely why one of them reacted so sharply.

Your concern about losing refunds may be completely valid. But a neutral administrative role shouldn’t be used to lobby panel members, especially right before a vote. It risks undermining trust in the minutes, in the process, and in you.

My advice: don’t double down. Repair it quickly and simply. You could say:

> “I realise I overstepped yesterday. I have strong views about the capped fee deal, but as minutes-taker I shouldn’t have tried to influence how you vote. I’ll keep my role neutral in panel discussions.”

That should be enough. You don’t need to apologise for your view itself — only for blurring the boundary.

Going forward, pick one lane:

- **If you want to campaign**, do it outside the panel setting: as a tenant, in writing, in a public meeting, or through a tenant group — not while taking minutes.
- **If you want to stay in the minutes role**, keep your opinions out of panel business. You can still raise factual concerns if asked, but avoid telling people how to vote.

If you feel strongly that the deal is bad, put that concern into a clear written statement from a tenant or campaign group, not into whispered pressure during panel work. That makes your objection legitimate and transparent instead of looking like backroom influence.

So: your politics weren’t the issue. Your position was.

Put the policy forward now, without the formal finding — but do not let it pass as a silent “fresh start.”

Your instinct is right that estate families were wronged. But your job at this moment is not to extract a confession from councillors who will not give one. It is to get the under-11s out of the car park before November turns into a longer winter. If you hold the line, you keep your moral position clean, but the people who suffer for it are the children and parents who need the facilities now. That is too high a price for a sentence in the minutes.

The better course is to pass the booking policy immediately, while putting something honest on the record that does not require the old guard to admit deliberate exclusion. Try wording like this:

> “The council acknowledges that, in practice, estate families have not had fair access to the rec and hall under previous booking arrangements. We regret that this has happened and adopt this policy to ensure fair, transparent access going forward.”

That is not “nobody’s fault.” It says the outcome was unfair. It does not say there was a conscious plot, which is the point the councillors cannot swallow. If they will not accept even that, make the policy motion plain and add a chair’s statement: “I personally believe past practice failed estate families, and I am moving this policy to correct that.” That gives the estate side a record of your position without making the council’s motion depend on a finding of intent.

Say something about the disrupted meeting too, but refuse both tribes’ scripts. Something like: “The alarm and shouting were unacceptable. But the frustration behind them was real and long-standing. We will not condone disruption, and we will not pretend the grievance was invented.”

Then act quickly: publish the new booking rules, give the estate group a named contact, set a review after one season, and track who gets Saturday slots. If the policy works, the record that matters most will be the football pitches in use.

No — you were not wrong to take it.

You made a hard, parental, practical choice: the children get the hall and the pitch in January. That is real. That changes Saturdays. That gives them something they were being denied. When you are dealing with an institution that has wronged you, sometimes the only honest victory available is the one that improves people’s lives now, even if it does not satisfy the need for justice later.

But I understand why people are angry. What hurts them is not that the children got access; it is that the council appears to have been allowed to say, “this was all just a misunderstanding,” while what the estate experienced feels deliberate, humiliating, and unacknowledged. Your sister may be grieving the fact that nobody has been made to say: this happened, and it was wrong.

So the answer is: you were right to secure the facility. You should not now let the council’s soft wording become the only story.

Do three things.

First, stop arguing with the estate about whether you betrayed them. Say plainly: “I took the deal because the kids needed the hall now. I do not agree that what happened was just a misunderstanding. I am not asking anyone to forgive the council.” That separates the practical win from moral surrender.

Second, make your own record. Write a short timeline: what was requested, what was refused, what was said, what changed, who was involved. Keep emails, notes of conversations, names, dates. Ask other parents to add their accounts. The council may not write the truth, but you can preserve it.

Third, push for a modest written safeguard going forward: the new booking rules, a named contact, a six-month review, and a clear complaints route if the estate is blocked again. You can ask the council to minute that “long-standing concerns about access were raised and the policy was revised,” without forcing them to admit malice.

Your sister may come round when she sees the children using the hall. Until then, don’t beg her to approve the deal. Tell her you are still holding the truth.

Take the three plots — but don’t lie about the other three.

The six-plot motion loses tonight. You know that. If you let it lose cleanly, the waiting families get nothing and the land stays derelict. A three-plot, two-year trial is not a sellout if it is written as a beachhead rather than a cap. It becomes a sellout only if you permanently surrender the remaining plots to protect your comfort or Derek’s pride.

So catch Derek before the meeting and give him a version he can own, but keep your language truthful. Say something like:

> “You’ve been right that doing all six at once is too risky. If you move a three-plot trial with strict stewardship conditions, I’ll back you and let you present it. The other three aren’t in tonight’s motion. They’re deferred, not allocated, and we’ll set a review date and clear criteria for expansion.”

Do not say “they’re off the table forever.” Say “they’re not in tonight’s motion” and “they’re deferred pending the trial.” That is true. It also gives Derek the safety he wants without forcing you to make a promise you know is false.

Let him present it. Let him call it careful stewardship. Let him take the win. If your ego is the price of getting fruit trees in the ground and a legitimate foothold for the families, pay it. You are not there to receive credit; you are there to get something real.

With the families, be honest before the vote if you can: “Six loses tonight. Three can pass, and it gives us a live trial, a record, and a review point. If we reject it, we get zero.” They may still be angry. Let them be angry. Their anger is about delay and scarcity, not about you personally. Do not promise them the full six; promise them that the trial will be designed so success makes expansion harder to refuse.

The amendment should include: three plots only, two-year term, named maintenance responsibilities, measurable success criteria, and a fixed date to reconsider the remaining plots. If Derek insists that the motion must permanently kill the other three, refuse that one point. But I suspect he will accept “deferred, reviewed later” if you give him the public victory.

Choose the imperfect gain over the clean defeat.

Send something tonight — but not a final verdict. Send a short holding message that stops the group becoming a courtroom. You are not deciding whether the whole arrangement survives while everyone is hot, tired, and fighting over £60. You are just stabilising it until Friday.

That is not a plaster. It is triage. If you try to hand down a full ruling now, they will treat it as another opening to argue. If you say only “I haven’t decided yet,” you are right: it may invite piling in. So be firmer than uncertainty, but less final than a decree.

Post something like:

“I’m not shutting the group, but I am changing how it’s used. This group is for Dad’s visits, meds and shopping, not money arguments. From tonight: the rota stands for now. Any disputes about petrol, cleaner or costs go to me privately, not in this thread. If anyone cannot continue with the rota, message me directly. I’ll review the longer-term setup after Dad’s appointment on Friday. Until then, please only reply here with rota/meds/visit updates.”

Then do not reopen it in the group tonight. If they push, repeat: “Send it to me privately. I’ll deal with it after Friday.” You do not need to answer every jab.

Privately, message your sister: “I hear you about starting again. Let’s get through Friday first, then we decide whether to reset.” Do not chase your cousin tonight unless there is a safety issue. If someone wants out, let them say so directly, but do not make the group perform loyalty in public.

Your job right now is not to be fair, liked, or decisive about everything. Your job is to keep Dad’s care from collapsing this week and stop the group feeding the conflict. After Friday, you can decide whether this arrangement is worth saving, whether only some siblings stay in, or whether you scrap it and build a smaller, clearer system with the people who will actually do the work. For tonight: contain, don’t conclude.

I’d go back in — but not to press for that teacher as a favour. Press for your son’s reading needs to be formally considered before placements are fixed.

Right now you’re mixing three things: a legitimate staff-admission policy, a class-placement request, and a personal debt/favour dynamic. The admission policy is defensible, but class allocation is different. Even if heads do move children around, asking for a specific teacher because she “owes you” is the part that can look improper, especially after that parent’s comments. It also puts the head in an awkward position: if she says yes, it may look like insider advantage; if she says no, it may feel personal.

So don’t leave it to chance, but change the ask. Send the head a short, parent-to-school message, not an office-colleague one. Say something like: “I’d like to discuss [son]’s reading progress and September class placement before decisions are final. He’s very distressed about reading and seems significantly behind. I want to make sure any placement decision is based on his support needs. Given my role, I want this handled through the normal parent process, not as a favour.”

In the meeting, focus on evidence: his reading level, phonics gaps, anxiety, crying over books, what support he currently gets, whether he needs assessment or intervention. You can mention the well-regarded teacher only lightly: “I know some parents speak highly of her for reading, but I’m asking what you think would best support him.” That lets the head connect the dots without being cornered.

Also ask for a concrete plan if he doesn’t get that class: targeted reading support, small-group phonics, assessment for learning difficulties, and a review date. The goal is not “best teacher by reputation” but “my child gets help.”

Don’t engage the other parents or the mum who complained. If it comes up, keep it boring: “I can’t discuss placements, but the school decides based on children’s needs.” And keep yourself completely out of any paperwork or decisions involving your own child.

Your instinct is right that silence may cost him. But push the needs case, not the favour.

You weren’t out of line for asking, but I’d be honest with yourself about why it landed badly with some parents.

Using the staff enrolment policy itself is legitimate. If the school offers that benefit to staff and you followed it properly, you don’t owe anyone an apology for taking a place you were entitled to apply for. Staff children being admitted under a policy is not the same as cutting the queue.

The teacher request is the more delicate part. Asking is not automatically wrong, especially if your son is behind with his reading and you genuinely believe he needs the strongest support. A head is allowed to take that into account, and she made the decision, not you. If she had felt it was inappropriate or unfair, she could have said no.

That said, from other parents’ point of view it can look like insider advantage: you already got the school place, then also got the “golden” teacher. Even if your request was reasonable, they may see it as staff getting first pick of a scarce resource. So I’d say: they’re probably annoyed it wasn’t them, but their annoyance isn’t entirely irrational. It’s less that you did something unethical, more that you benefited from proximity and access that other parents don’t have.

My advice would be not to defend it as a right or make it sound like staff families deserve special treatment. If it comes up again, keep it simple: “I asked because he’s struggling with reading and I was worried about him. The head made the call.” Don’t over-explain, don’t apologise, but don’t rub it in either.

Also, I’d quietly check with the school that the placement is based on his needs rather than just your request. If he is behind, make sure he gets proper reading support regardless of which teacher he has. That way, if anyone questions it later, the answer is clear: you advocated for your child’s learning needs, not just for status or convenience.

Do not put the monthly dinner forward as if it is the plan you now believe in. Put it forward as a funded trial, with the weekly need still stated plainly.

The difference matters. If you say, “This is my plan,” you let two board members conclude you inflated the need. If you say, “The assessed need is weekly; the board’s current appetite is monthly; I propose a three-month monthly pilot with a review,” you keep the truth intact and still give them an easy yes.

Tell the coordinator beforehand: “I’ll bring the smaller version, but I can’t present it as the full answer. I’ll call it a staged start.” She wants something passable; this is passable. At the meeting, make the motion small and concrete: one dinner a month for three months, a capped budget, a review date, and a request that the common room stay open and lit after ten on those nights. Ask one of the sceptical board members to attend and help serve—not to inspect, but to meet the people. You don’t need to name the Samoan cutter; describe the lingering by the washing machines, the rooms that are only bunk, kettle and silence.

Then use the dinner as evidence. Keep a simple record: how many come, how long they stay, whether they take food back to mates, what they ask for next. If the room fills, return after three dinners with actual costs and say, “This worked, and it confirmed the need is weekly.” If it does not fill, you have learned something without pretending the ache was monthly.

Meanwhile, separate what the board must pay from what the district can carry. Ask orchardists, the packing shed, a church, RSL, Lions, or a supermarket for gas, meat, fruit, bread, phone credit, or decks of cards. If you can cover the extras outside the budget, the weekly version becomes less frightening to the foundation. You are not shutting up; you are learning how money moves while still saying what loneliness does.

So: yes to the monthly dinner. No to calling it enough. Take the yes, cook properly, keep the room warm, and make the next step visible. That is practical.

Tell her to put the smaller figure on the first line—but only as the amount you are asking the panel to approve now, not as the true total of need.

The first line is not the moral ledger. It is the motion. If two panel members have already said the larger ask is dead, putting the full costed sum first is a gesture. It lets you feel honest while Noor’s cousin, the family from the camp, and anyone else likely to miss a tribunal get nothing. The smaller figure is the one that can become actual bus fare, actual tickets, actual appearances.

But do not make Mara write the exclusion alone. When she asks, say: “Put the smaller number as the request. Label it ‘capped emergency travel fund’ or ‘pilot allocation.’ Then add one line: ‘Documented need to date is higher; this request funds the highest-priority cases under the criteria below.’” If the panel wants only one page, keep the criteria tight: imminent hearing/appeal deadline, no other source of funds, lowest reasonable fare, and first-come or greatest hardship. If Noor’s cousin and the camp family fit those criteria, they should be inside it.

You also need to fix the expectations Mara has already created. Today, send or say jointly: “We are submitting a capped proposal. It may not pass, and it may not cover everyone.” Do not let her keep two people believing a yes is near just because you are trying to keep the packet clean.

Most important: own the number. Don’t hand her the pen and call it her draft. Say, “I chose the smaller figure because it is the only one likely to survive. I will present the cap and answer for it. You present the evidence.” That is not the same as making her mark whose door stays shut.

This is triage, not betrayal. Ask for the survivable amount, name the larger need if there is any space, and take responsibility for the limit. If the panel later asks why the folder shows more, tell the truth: the need is real; this is what can pass now.
